utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could we please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, Dr. Cornish, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood for the Prosecution, assisted by Alma Imamovic-Ivanov our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to my colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Rasim Delic, with our legal assistant Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Good morning, Dr. Cornish. May I just remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you made at the commencement of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Cornish. I started out yesterday with my last question, and I'm going to put it to you now. Doctor, you told us that for a leader to be able to command and control his army efficiently, he needs to be fed information about what is happening below him, underneath him. I asked yesterday what are the principles governing the passing of information from below upwards, and you told us that there were really no rules, but, of course, everything essential needed to be passed up, so that the information that finally gets to the Supreme Commander would enable this commander to take the appropriate measures to carry on with the battle. My question to you is: What do you do if the system doesn't work, if the information that is being passed up is incorrect or insufficient, meaning that, through all or at each of the levels, essential information is dropped, doesn't get further, is being sifted away for reasons that you don't know? What's the commander to do then and can he be held responsible?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might beginning by making two comments which I think are germane to my response. The first is to say that the passage of information, as I think I touched on yesterday, should always be a balance of speed, on the one hand, and accuracy, on the other. The ideal would to be have all information passed up to as near as instantly as possible, but that obviously isn't going to be achievable; and, therefore, you have a system of warning and alerting followed by a system of providing more information as time makes it possible. It is that point about system, you said, sir, quite rightly that there are no rules in this, quite obviously. There is plenty of system. There are plenty of procedures and processes by which information should be passed. As I said yesterday, I think, an army in combat can be curiously and counter-intuitively quite a bureaucratic system. It doesn't look as if it ought to be that way, but it often can be. Going directly to the question, when this system doesn't work, when it is imperfect, as I guess it must most of the time be given the circumstances, that's when you come to the point at which the commander has to make judgments on the basis of what does know and on the information that he does have. I think this comes back to our discussion yesterday when, I think, we went into the higher realms of Western strategy and Clausewitz, and the idea that the commander has to have the confidence to take responsibility for his command. That, in a sense, is what this person has been trained to do. The system ought to run perfectly or it would be good if it ran perfectly and provided everything. But we all know, and circumstances will suggest; that at times, perhaps more often than not, he will not have perfect information; therefore, he has to make the best judgment he can. It follows from that when more information does then come that might change the picture in front of him, he should, again, in a position and have the confidence to change his plan and adapt to what he knows. It is difficult to describe, I think, in concrete terms, but I think it is a matter of judgment and confidence interplaying all the time with the information that is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply, which raises a question about the duty of the Supreme Commander to actively seek information from below if, for any reason, he has suspicions about the efficiency of the information that is being passed up to him. My question is really: Do commanders have a special duty to actively seek information about what is going on underneath him, but, more precisely, because that is what leaders also should do, I guess, about crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, sir, in general, I would say that the commander at any level would have such a duty. That is, after all, why he has been put in this position. I've been saying that he needs information and intelligence, and this person knows that he needs that information and intelligence; therefore, it follows there must be some duty on him to provide it. But I would say two things: The first is that, in a sense, that duty is largely executed in the form of the commander ensuring that the system below him is functioning, and the way he achieves that is by ensuring that he has the right people in the right positions below and around him. That is precisely the idea behind command chain and hierarchical structures and so on. This one person cannot be everywhere all the time, so his duty is, in a sense, manifested in ensuring that he has a functioning commander chain. I think the other thing I would say is that the duty aspect of this works in two directions; that's to say, this is a system in which every level of the hierarchy is functioning under a duty, and it is the duty of junior commanders to ensure that their senior has the information. So, in a sense - and I know I'm beginning to portray that, as we said yesterday, begins to look as if it might be a perfect model - but, in a sense, the idea behind this is that it should be a self-correcting system. If there is an problem somewhere, then something ought to be down to correct it and ensure that the information is passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Cornish, could I take you to the very first question that the Prosecutor asked you yesterday, relating to this part of the military group which refuses to wear uniforms yet carries out commands in combat. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to add another variable to that equation and ask for your comment, and the variable that I would like to add is, that same paramilitary group, what would your comment be if, in fact, it does not belong to the same national group as the army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Once again, if I might take the opportunity to preface my answer with my one remark, which is to say that, in essence, my comments on the paramilitary hypothesis were that coincidence of effort, military effort, might be seen by the local commander to be a good thing, but that commander would also know that coincidence of effort is not the same as unity of effort in the military sense. Again, going directly to your question, sir, if the paramilitary group is not of the same nationality, then I would say that the -- the problems, or at least the unease that I commented on and expressed yesterday, I think would be magnified a number of times, because it might then be possible that, as well as not wearing the uniform and not using the same insignia and the flags and all these other paraphernalia of military activity, there might then be a grave problem of a lack of common language, in which case, as I said yesterday, there are or there would ordinarily be special mechanisms to try and cater for that problem. But it seems to me that if this paramilitary organisation were both distinct and of another language, that there would be next to no chance of organizing proper liaison functions and so on, simply because it would not be trained in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall I just add another factor; whereas, there is an problem of language, there is interpretation. This is an interpreter who helps.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, that moderates the problem somewhat, sir. But I would then go back to my earlier comment that this remains a paramilitary organisation, which, I think, we agreed yesterday or the hypothesis went yesterday, that it might even be paid from some other source and replenished by some other non-standard means. And in those circumstances, I would say that this body looks far closer to a mercenary organisation that happens to be operating on the same battlefield and might be providing a coincidence of effort. But in my judgment, on the basis of knowledge and understanding of these matters, it would be difficult to equate that with a formed part of the same hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday, Judge Harhoff asked you if you know how would the regular army's military police handle crimes or violations of international humanitarian law committed by a paramilitary unit. You said you have no doubt acknowledge it, but you think this would be a very large-scale challenge, because the system that we are talking about would have a certain capability in military police and military discipline that would be predicated on their there being a general disciplined understanding of what to do and what not to do. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you gave us this answer, I was keen to hear how you would suggest how this situation could be handled though, and your answer did not go as far as handling that situation and dealing with that situation.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So to be clear, we, in my own mind, we have a paramilitary organisation of some sort which might or might not be of the same nationality and the same linguistic grouping, albeit with translators; and there is an suggestion that this organisation might have committed a grave violation. The problem that I see is that the military police and investigative capacities of, if you like, our model army is limited, as I said yesterday, in its capacity; and I think there would also - and here, forgive me, but you know I don't have a legal background - but it seems to me that there would be a very pressing problem of jurisdiction here: Precisely what is this organisation, what is the jurisdiction, and who has jurisdiction over that body in the case of this alleged crime. In a sense, Your Honour, I'm not answering your question because I'm really not -- I've not come across this scenario, this hypothesis before. But those seem to be the sort of practical and jurisdictional problems that could prove to be so overwhelming at that time that, in effect, our model army's command structure would simply be unable to address the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the piecemeal supply of information to you. Let me extend the scenario so as to enable you to deal with the jurisdictional problem. This paramilitary group, what would you say if it was actually subordinated and incorporated into the army.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it had been fully incorporated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is an order that subordinates it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which case, I would suppose that the command structure would have worked out, or would have calculated, that all aspects of the support and disciplining of that paramilitary structure would have been thought through. What I mean here is, if it is to be fully integrated, then it needs fuel just as it much as it might need the back-up from the military police requirement. So there should be a sense in which it does not stretch the capacity of our model army too far. I think that would be my answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in that scenario, you talked about mercenaries a little earlier when Judge Harhoff was talking to you; and without suggesting that this paramilitary group that we are talking about would or would not be a mercenary group, what would your answer be to the question of the responsibility of the commander of the army over this group? Would the commanders of the army be responsible for any crimes committed by this group?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour - and I'm straying here into an area in which I'm not expert - my understanding is that the idea of command responsibility is still developing, and I think this might be one of the examples where we can see just how undeveloped it is. I think it would essentially depend on the extent to which this paramilitary organisation had been integrated and had been seen to be integrated. How far had this organisation agreed to accept and abide by the frameworks of discipline, logistics, and all these other aspects of the military command structure; and had it not accepted those, then I think we would come back to the same problem. How much jurisdiction can be assumed by our commander, because let's not forget, that the commander, in a sense, in any combat situation is relying on a very great deal of assumed jurisdiction. This doesn't have to be said. It is simply axiomatic that he is in command and that he has authority, both of the military and jurisdiction sort, over these he commands. If these assumptions cannot be made in these pressing circumstances, then I think it could be difficult. And if I could make one final point. I use the term mercenary, by which I meant, I suppose that there might be some uncertainty about how and why these paramilitary troops were being paid. That would create a certain impression among the ranks of our model army. They would see an organisation that appeared to be being paid perhaps better, perhaps more quickly, whatever, from somewhere else; and, very quickly, the term "mercenary" I think, would begin to be used, and that would have certain implications as far as morale and everything else is concerned. But more to the point, the fact that this organisation is receiving pay from outside would symbolise, I think very powerfully that it was not part of the overall organised command structure and could not, therefore, be fully integrated; and it was not part of an alliance either and, therefore, was in a separate category all on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Cornish. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just one issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Dr. Cornish, yesterday, His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you about how information would be sent up through the various layers of command and the way that this information would be condensed; and, again, His Honour touched upon it this morning. Yesterday, you said that no rules applied, and you said that it would involve an officer at a level having a close sense of what the next level commander would require. If I can ask you about the senior professional head of the army, sitting at the top of the army structure at the strategic level, what level of detail would you expect to find in the information coming up to that man?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the term "no rules apply" is an interesting one in retrospect; and I think I would stand by that term, but I would embellish it, if I might, by saying this: There is, in a sense, a realistic expectation that, no matter how many rules you have, it probably won't be possible for those rules to be met; therefore, there is it an emphasis on the systems and processes which I described a little while ago. It would be good if the rules could apply but they won't, so we have to some more dynamic and realistic sense of a way of going about things. As to the professional head of the army, sitting there in his capital, he really would expect the most general picture but with very little detail, because the assumption would be that the detail is properly the concern of much more subordinate commanders than him; and if he were to be involving himself with a very high level of detail, it could look as if he were checking on the subordinates or perhaps even be in a position of being about to contradict them with orders or something. So should keep distant from that level of detail; allow it to be dealt with at the proper level wherever it might be, platoon or brigade or division; and should concern himself with bigger ideas, and his thinking upwards to his political level. What he should be especially concerned with is the detail of a grave problem that arises. That should come back through the system to him, if, for example, as a two or three levels below him, it transpires that mechanized divisions have all of a sudden -- it has completely impossible to find any fuel, there is none available to be requisitioned, and none of the allies are providing it, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. That becomes a grave matter of pressing detail that is right that he should be about; but, otherwise, it should be dealt with at the level at which it can be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have, Dr. Cornish, just a couple of questions, but let me pick up with where my learned colleague Mr. Robson left off. In this situation where the Supreme Commander, the overall commander, has this large staff working for him, one would assume that information coming to them is going to be further filtered and made known to the commander when those issues are of importance, wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would sir. It's not something which I have seen at close hand, but my imagination and understanding suggests that the our Supreme Commander would be given a general impression and would be told only if there was something urgently problematic that he needed to know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In fact, that is the whole point of having that staff around that commander who is receiving -- that staff receiving information from the field, so that all problems can be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would agree with that precisely, sir. I would say, thought, that we shouldn't forget that this very, very high level of the command structure, our Supreme Command, is more about the organisation and equipment of our model army than about the operational direction of it, and it shouldn't actually be about the operational direction of it. That is to do with people who are in the theatre of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But certainly that overall the Supreme Commander is going to have strategic responsibilities with respect to what is go on?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, would you not agree with me that notwithstanding this structure where this is an staff, where information is coming to the staff, in no means does that staff structure permit that overall commander to forgo or not be responsible for what happens?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think would agree with your earlier statement, sir, that the very idea of the staff structure is so that he is actually able to be better briefed and in control of the whole thing. That is why he has the staff around him. I think I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that staff structure is put in place precisely so that Supreme Commander can exercise the authority that is vested in him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And so that he can be accountable to the political leadership for what goes on in the army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so. Again, at that level, it must go both ways. He needs to represent the army to the political level, and he needs also to ensure that, to the extent it is relevant, that the political message is going down to the right level in the command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn, sir, to the last issue I'd like to talk to you about, and this concerns some questions and answers that were put to you this morning, concerning paramilitary groups and/or mercenaries. If there was an order subordinating a paramilitary group into the army, you would not characterise such a paramilitary group as a mercenary group, would you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think I would. I think I would assume, in the scenario that you paint, that the important tests would have been passed, that this organisation would be integrated in the circumstances that we referred to in logistics and so on, and discipline, and perhaps even, but not necessarily, in terms of uniform and insignia. I think it might be, therefore, right to assume that there would be a single command chain and unity of command and all of the other things spoke been yesterday; and, indeed, that there would be no uncertainty about payment, so picking up all the other things that we have been touching on in this scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I think, sir, the final question is whether your view on this issue of this paramilitary group or mercenary group, is this any different if the request to be subordinated to the army came from that paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think probably not, because, again, thinking yesterday to our discussion yesterday, we can all conceive that in times of crisis and confrontation that there might be a miniature levee en masse, that there might some civilians or some reasonably armed people turning up an offering services. And, in a way, it would have to be regarded in that sort of light. The commander of our new model army meeting these people in the field would or should, in my estimate, be asking him self: Who are people, how well are they trained, where did they come from, how long are they staying, can I trust them, et cetera, et cetera. And if unable to answer those questions, then I would think he would be forgiven for not relying on that organisation overly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me take part of your answer and take it again a little bit further. You talked about or you just answered "reasonably armed people turning up and offering services," and this is on line 15 of page 14. These reasonably armed people turning up and offering services. If that group of reasonably armed people who turned up and offered their services proposed themselves to be a unit of the army and an order then resulted forming them into a unit of the army, what conclusions would you draw in that situation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not, I'm afraid, all that different from those I've just painted. This body of people, let's say they are wearing crisp new uniforms and they look well equipped, and they all have an assault rifle, let's say, and perhaps even various other weapons, my point would be that none of those things are actually all that difficult to get hold of. They are all available on a market somewhere. Therefore, we come back to the same challenge to the commander in place: I know nothing about these people, I know nothing about what they can do. They have asked if they can become part of my brigade; and, to be honest, I would be completely mad to allow that happen. I might, though, as I said yesterday, I might involve them, let us say, in a defensive position or as part of an overall operation, but I would expect to disperse them among my own resources, rather than rely upon them specifically in one area or for one task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, I'm not clear being in my question. My question goes, sir, to these reasonably armed people who turn up, offer their services, request to be formed into a unit, and the commander, in fact, does issue an order forming them into a unit. What conclusions would you reach -- the commander, in other words, issues that order forming them into a unit.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. In which case, he has satisfied himself that all those tests have been passed: That this organisation can be fully integrated into his command chain, that it understands the command chain, that it -- its training background and military capacity is of a certain level that would be useful and could be integrated with his own force. All those tests having been passed, it might be in his judgment to integrate it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Cornish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Cornish, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much taking time off your very busy schedule to come and testify to the Tribunal to testify. You are now excused, and you now stand down. Please travel well back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The window is open, we are not in open session. Madam Vidovic, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I have been informed by the registrar, the witness is a witness of the Prosecution, whom we have called for additional examination; and as communication was not allowed with him, we have been informed by the registrar's office that the witness is coming today and we plan to have him testify tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. In that event, then the Court stands adjourned to tomorrow 9.00 in the morning, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of April, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.37 a.m.,
